text: After this you can evaluate whether the change process itself is being followed.

Product evidence and process evidence answer different questions. A correct item can result despite skipped reviews. A tidy procedure can still produce a nonconforming item. A process check samples requests, decisions, releases and closures. It tests whether the stated controls were followed. Trace a few examples end to end, including one rejected or pending request.

items: Choose a small set of change records with different outcomes. You should see: The sample includes more than successful approvals. If not: Include unusual or delayed cases where useful.
Follow each request from entry to current state. You should see: Review, decision and release evidence can be connected. If not: Record breaks in the trail.
Compare actual steps with the agreed process. You should see: Skipped or ambiguous controls are visible. If not: Ask whether a documented exception applies.
Report the process risk and needed correction. You should see: The finding names a condition and supporting example. If not: Avoid claiming the sample proves every transaction is identical.
In one sample, a software update could have a signed decision but no revised user instruction. That indicates a release-process gap even if the software works.

text: Test the process with actual records, not assurances that a process exists.
A small sample gives limited confidence about overall frequency.

items: Equating an approved plan with proof of compliance The real workflow may differ. Fix: Trace completed transactions and exceptions.
